analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 15% minimum tax on corporations earning over $1 billion in profits.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 15% minimum tax on the largest corporations has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no vote since it was referred there in February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law requires corporations that average more than $1 billion in profits to pay a minimum 15% tax on the income they report to shareholders, no matter how many deductions they use to lower their tax bill. This bill wipes out that minimum tax entirely and lets those corporations use all their credits and deductions again. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest U.S. corporations — the ones averaging more than $1 billion in profits — gain the most, because they would no longer owe the 15% minimum tax on book income and could use tax credits without a cap [S2][S3]. Wealthy shareholders also benefit indirectly, since lower corporate taxes can lift stock prices.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 15% corporate alternative minimum tax, which under current law applies to corporations with adjusted financial statement income (book income) averaging over $1 billion for three consecutive years [S2][S3].
Removes the related limit on how much of the general business tax credit a corporation can use, so large corporations could claim credits currently curtailed by the minimum tax [S2][S3].
Applies retroactively in effect: the repeal takes effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: the federal government collects less revenue from the largest profitable corporations, which means larger deficits or higher taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing costs borne by everyone else. Ordinary taxpayers whose income comes mostly from wages — and who cannot restructure earnings to avoid tax — do not get an equivalent benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: All taxpayers, through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the only tax that guarantees the roughly 100 largest profitable corporations pay at least a 15% rate on reported profits, meaning corporations with big paper profits and large deductions could again owe little or no federal income tax [S2].
Repealing a revenue-raising tax adds to federal deficits unless Congress replaces the money, shifting the burden toward future taxpayers and other programs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to a small set of the largest corporations and their shareholders, while the cost — lower federal revenue — is spread across everyone through deficits or offsetting cuts. The bill offers no direct benefit to ordinary working people, and the honest case for it (a simpler tax code) could be pursued with narrower reforms instead of full repeal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2025, and it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. John Barrasso introduced the Book Minimum Tax Repeal Act on February 27, 2025 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, with no further action recorded [S5].
Eight Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained: the 15% minimum tax on the largest corporations remains law while the repeal sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the tax still applies

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 8 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill (Sens. Crapo, Lankford, Cassidy, Daines, Blackburn, Ricketts, Risch, and Lummis).

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has joined, so support splits entirely by party.

industries.industry: Largest U.S. corporations (averaging over $1 billion in book income, including big tech, pharmaceutical, and energy firms)
industries.note: The bill would exempt them from the 15% minimum tax on profits they report to shareholders and lift the cap on tax credits they can use [S2][S3]. The gain comes out of federal revenue, so their benefit is paid for by the public through larger deficits or offsetting cuts.
Lower corporate tax bills can raise after-tax returns and stock values, concentrating the benefit among those who hold the most stock.

analysis.trajectory: With no Democratic support and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is unlikely to get a standalone vote. Large corporate tax changes in this Congress are more likely to move through the budget reconciliation process than through a bill like this one.
